identity.jurisdiction: Saskatchewan health system with federal legal context

owner_view.what_happened: A Saskatoon Health Region-commissioned external review documented the reported experiences of seven Indigenous women who described pressure or coercion around tubal ligation. The review treated those accounts as a cohort/systemic concern, issued ten Calls to Action, and was followed by an apology, legal proceedings and a hospital-based Indigenous birth-support response.
why_this_matters: The case shows how anonymized lived experience can become a formal health-system accountability record without identifying patients.
It connects institutional findings to a concrete operational service while preserving that one program does not satisfy all ten Calls to Action.
Later litigation and federal legislation must be kept procedurally and temporally distinct from the 2017 review.
review_first: The 2017 review's ten Calls to Action remain the canonical accountability baseline.
The Indigenous Birth Support Worker program is a verified operational response, but it is only a partial response to a broader set of recommended structural reforms.
Popp v Canada certification was dismissed in 2025 on class-definition/common-issue/preferability grounds; that is not a merits finding that the reported sterilizations did or did not occur.
review_next: No current public ten-action implementation ledger was located.
Confirm whether an appeal followed the 2025 certification decision.
Seek policy-level evidence for the review's consent-policy and governance recommendations.
Keep Bill S-228 as later contextual federal law only.
reference: Saskatoon is in Treaty 6 territory and the Homeland of the Métis; that is territorial context, not a legal-right conclusion in this dossier.
what_we_know: The commissioned review records seven anonymized patient accounts and interviews with nine providers.
The report issued ten Calls to Action spanning rights, training, governance, workforce, supports, reparation, reproductive support and consent policy.
SHA states that the birth-support program was created in response and is operational at Jim Pattison Children's Hospital.
A 2025 court decision dismissed class certification at that procedural stage.
what_remains_uncertain: Current implementation status for most of the ten Calls to Action.
Whether an appeal or successor collective proceeding followed the 2025 decision.
Whether consent-policy changes were adopted and audited across Saskatchewan.
How the legal claims will proceed, if at all, as individual actions.
next_questions: Can SHA provide a current implementation table for all ten Calls to Action?
Was 2025 SKKB 89 appealed or followed by a reconfigured proceeding?
owner_view.recommended_next_move: Request or locate a current SHA ten-Call-to-Action implementation ledger, with special focus on consent policy, Indigenous governance and workforce recommendations.
owner_view.one_thing_to_remember: A real, current birth-support service is documented, but it should not be mistaken for completion of the review's wider structural agenda.

investigation_and_findings.title: Commissioned external review
investigation_and_findings.summary: Seven anonymized women and nine providers were interviewed; the review documented a cohort/systemic pattern and ten Calls to Action.

recommendations.title: Ten Calls to Action
recommendations.summary: Rights and UNDRIP-informed care; mandatory education; equal Indigenous governance partnership; advisory authority; representative workforce; coordinated supports; reparation; reproductive support; and revised, monitored consent policy.

legal_policy_context.title: Saskatchewan health-system consent and governance responsibilities
legal_policy_context.summary: The review directly called for revised tubal-ligation and consent policy and structural Indigenous partnership.
legal_policy_context.boundary: The present dossier does not claim provincewide adoption without later authoritative policy evidence.

legal_policy_context.title: Popp v Canada legal process
legal_policy_context.summary: The litigation is a legal accountability process related to alleged coerced sterilizations.
legal_policy_context.boundary: The 2025 certification dismissal is procedural and not a merits ruling about individual allegations.

legal_policy_context.title: Bill S-228 / S.C. 2026, c. 10
legal_policy_context.summary: The Criminal Code amendment is relevant to the national legal response to coerced sterilization.
legal_policy_context.boundary: Later contextual legal development only; it is not retroactively applied and no direct case-specific remedy is inferred.

legal_policy_context.title: Treaty 6 and Métis Homeland
legal_policy_context.summary: The location context is accurate and useful for governance research.
legal_policy_context.boundary: No treaty-right or jurisdictional conclusion is inferred from geography.

funding.title: Indigenous Birth Support Worker Program
funding.summary: The program's operation is documented; no service-level funding amount was located in this bounded pass.

implementation_evidence.summary: The institutional apology is documented through official/parliamentary context but is not implementation of all Calls to Action.
SHA states that the Indigenous Birth Support Worker Program was created in response to the review.
A current SHA page confirms the service remains accessible at Jim Pattison Children's Hospital.
SHA reported evaluation findings and improvement/scale recommendations.

follow_up_and_recurrence.title: Federal committee and later legislation
follow_up_and_recurrence.summary: Later federal scrutiny revisited consent, data, guidance and accountability concerns; repetition is a signal, not proof of non-implementation.

follow_up_and_recurrence.title: Class certification
follow_up_and_recurrence.summary: Certification was dismissed in 2025; individual merits were not adjudicated by that result.

findings.uncertainty: It only addresses part of a much broader reform agenda.
findings.recommended_action: Preserve the source-backed link but do not label all Calls to Action implemented.

findings.title: Certification status is now known
findings.summary: 2025 SKKB 89 dismissed class certification on procedural criteria.
findings.why_it_matters: It materially updates a stale legal-status gap.
findings.uncertainty: Appeal or successor proceeding status was not located.
findings.recommended_action: Confirm appellate/docket status before public use.

findings.title: Most Calls to Action lack current disaggregated status
findings.summary: No current public ten-action ledger was located.
findings.why_it_matters: Consent policy and governance reforms are central, not incidental.
findings.uncertainty: Missing public evidence is not proof of non-implementation.
findings.recommended_action: Seek a bounded SHA implementation table.

findings.title: Later federal law must remain contextual
findings.why_it_matters: It is important legal context without being a case-specific remedy.
findings.recommended_action: Keep a visible temporal/legal boundary in the dossier.

knowledge_gap_follow_ups.question: What is the current public procedural status of the proposed class action?
knowledge_gap_follow_ups.answer: The Court of King's Bench dismissed certification in Popp v Canada (Attorney General), 2025 SKKB 89. An appeal or successor collective proceeding was not located.
knowledge_gap_follow_ups.stopping_reason: An authoritative case digest resolves the certification stage. Targeted official and case-law searches did not locate an appeal, and further open-web searching showed diminishing returns.

owner_assessment.owner_review_reason: Current status for most Calls to Action and any post-2025 appeal require owner review.
owner_assessment.recommended_next_action: Prioritize an SHA recommendation-status follow-up and court-docket verification.

limitations: The dossier preserves anonymous cohort evidence and distinguishes allegation, review finding, institutional response, program operation, court procedure and later law. It does not identify patients, adjudicate individual claims or infer implementation from silence.
